source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5

coverage.syllabusReading: pp. 225–284 is first rulemaking range; file ends p. 283
coverage.status: Notice of proposals and disclosure of supporting data, including full opinions and unsolved hypotheticals

topics.title: § 5.3.1 — NPRM, Notice Adequacy & Logical Outgrowth (pp. 246–254)
topics.description: Administrative Procedure Act § 553(b), Chocolate Manufacturers, alternative final rules, Long Island Care, state modifications, lead-exposure problem.

entries.title: APA § 553(b): minimum content of proposed-rule notice
entries.summary: NPRM must state terms or substance of proposed rule or describe subjects and issues involved; notice must fairly allow interested persons to comment.
entries.laymanExplanation: NPRM must state terms or substance of proposed rule or describe subjects and issues involved; notice must fairly allow interested persons to comment.
entries.legalExplanation: The agency must clearly signal the regulatory possibilities it is considering. Reading a notice should help interested people know whether and what to submit.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 248–250
entries.examApplication: Evaluate original text and preamble, regulatory history, foreseeable alternate outcomes and whether outsiders had meaningful chance to contribute.
entries.examTrap: Publishing an NPRM does not authorize arbitrary unanticipated changes later.

entries.title: § 553(c): public submissions and agency learning
entries.summary: Notice-and-comment procedures allow affected persons to submit relevant facts and arguments so agency can make a reasoned choice; agency remains free to revise proposals in response to comments.
entries.laymanExplanation: Notice-and-comment procedures allow affected persons to submit relevant facts and arguments so agency can make a reasoned choice; agency remains free to revise proposals in response to comments.
entries.legalExplanation: A proposal should be open enough to improve based on new information, but not so vague that impacted groups miss the chance to be heard.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 248–249
entries.examApplication: Substantial comments require genuine consideration, not necessarily adoption; courts weigh whether opportunity was real.

entries.title: Chocolate Manufacturers Association v. Block, 755 F.2d 1098 (4th Cir. 1985)
entries.summary: No. In the particular regulatory setting, interested producers lacked fair notice of potential removal; Fourth Circuit reversed and directed agency to reopen comments.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. In the particular regulatory setting, interested producers lacked fair notice of potential removal; Fourth Circuit reversed and directed agency to reopen comments.
entries.legalExplanation: Was a final ban on flavored milk a logical outgrowth of notice that explicitly permitted flavored milk and never put milk flavoring at issue? Agency may adapt after public input, but final change must be in character with the noticed scheme and reasonably foreseeable. Previous program use, preamble's detailed other food sugar discussion and affirmative permission for flavored milk misled interested commenters into thinking the question was settled.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 246–250
entries.sourceRole: Case opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: USDA proposed revised WIC food packages after congressional sugar, salt and fat directive. Proposal explicitly retained flavored or unflavored milk and discussed reducing sugar in cereals and juice, not milk. Seventy-eight of more than 1,000 commenters requested removal of flavored milk. USDA final rule deleted it without allowing interested parties specific further comment.
entries.issue: Was a final ban on flavored milk a logical outgrowth of notice that explicitly permitted flavored milk and never put milk flavoring at issue?
entries.holding: No. In the particular regulatory setting, interested producers lacked fair notice of potential removal; Fourth Circuit reversed and directed agency to reopen comments.
entries.reasoning: Agency may adapt after public input, but final change must be in character with the noticed scheme and reasonably foreseeable. Previous program use, preamble's detailed other food sugar discussion and affirmative permission for flavored milk misled interested commenters into thinking the question was settled.
entries.rule: The final rule must be a logical outgrowth of an adequate NPRM and comments: it may differ but cannot materially shift issues without fair warning and opportunity for participation.
entries.examApplication: For exam, set out what NPRM actually said about milk; contrast general sugar concerns with item-specific preservation; identify harm to those who would have opposed exclusion.
entries.examTrap: Case does not prohibit all reversals between proposal and final rule; it applies context-specific fair notice standard.

entries.title: Logical-outgrowth test as a two-way constraint
entries.summary: Final regulation must be reasonably foreseeable from NPRM and subjects genuinely under discussion, not a surprise material departure; otherwise agency must reopen notice/comment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Final regulation must be reasonably foreseeable from NPRM and subjects genuinely under discussion, not a surprise material departure; otherwise agency must reopen notice/comment.
entries.legalExplanation: The final rule can change, but commenters should have been alerted to its possibility.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 248–253
entries.examApplication: Some courts phrase as final changes 'in character with original scheme.' The goal is fair public notice and ability to present information relevant to policy adopted.
entries.examTrap: Compare original notice, final text, nature and size of change, affected classes, and accessible comments.

entries.title: Material departure versus ordinary refinement
entries.summary: Need not identify every variant of every final provision; revising figures or implementing suggested alternatives may be valid if notice genuinely presented the relevant choices.
entries.laymanExplanation: Need not identify every variant of every final provision; revising figures or implementing suggested alternatives may be valid if notice genuinely presented the relevant choices.
entries.legalExplanation: Do not force another round for every modest textual edit, but major unrelated proposals need fresh notice.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 248–250
entries.examApplication: Courts examine policy of participation rather than magic words. Challenge stronger where agency unequivocally announced a practice would continue.
entries.examTrap: Compare stakes, delta between proposed/final, and how a reasonable affected reader perceived proposed scope.

entries.title: Advance notices of proposed rulemaking (ANPRMs)
entries.summary: Before formal NPRM, agencies may solicit preliminary input, consult private standards bodies, advisory committees and affected groups.
entries.laymanExplanation: Before formal NPRM, agencies may solicit preliminary input, consult private standards bodies, advisory committees and affected groups.
entries.legalExplanation: Predesign consultations can improve proposal but usually do not substitute for legally required NPRM.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 250

entries.title: Unified Agenda and regulatory planning
entries.summary: Executive Order 12,866 described semiannual listing of regulations under development and upcoming significant federal actions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Executive Order 12,866 described semiannual listing of regulations under development and upcoming significant federal actions.
entries.legalExplanation: A planning agenda helps people anticipate future proposals; it is not itself a final rule or a substitute for § 553 notice.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 250

entries.title: Long Island Care at Home v. Coke, 551 U.S. 158 (2007)
entries.summary: Supreme Court approved final third-party companionship-worker exemption though initial proposal would have retained FLSA coverage for some third-party employees.
entries.laymanExplanation: Supreme Court approved final third-party companionship-worker exemption though initial proposal would have retained FLSA coverage for some third-party employees.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court found proposal's reversal reasonably foreseeable: proposed treatment itself announced issue under agency consideration.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 251–252
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast Chocolate Manufacturers' affirmative retention and silence about milk removal.

entries.title: Environmental Integrity Project v. EPA, 425 F.3d 992 (D.C. Cir. 2005)
entries.summary: Casebook notes a proposed interpretation's complete reversal may fall outside logical outgrowth, depending on notice.
entries.laymanExplanation: Casebook notes a proposed interpretation's complete reversal may fall outside logical outgrowth, depending on notice.
entries.legalExplanation: Use as counterexample to broad Long Island Care U-turn acceptance.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 252
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Analyze how precisely agency signaled alternatives.

entries.title: Agency notice versus comments as constructive notice
entries.summary: Some courts emphasize legal notice must originate in agency NPRM rather than only appear in public submissions, even if comments are posted online.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some courts emphasize legal notice must originate in agency NPRM rather than only appear in public submissions, even if comments are posted online.
entries.legalExplanation: An obscure third-party comment is not necessarily notice to the entire affected public that the agency considers a new outcome.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 252
entries.examApplication: Horsehead and other cases illustrate debate whether publicly accessible comments can broaden permissible final rule.
entries.examTrap: Do not simply assume all comments independently amend the agency's notice.

entries.title: Horsehead Resource Development v. Browner, 16 F.3d 1246 (D.C. Cir. 1994)
entries.summary: Book cites proposition notice ordinarily must come from the agency itself.
entries.laymanExplanation: Book cites proposition notice ordinarily must come from the agency itself.
entries.legalExplanation: Supports scrutiny of final proposals arising first in third-party submissions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 252
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Look for explicit agency solicitation or broad enough NPRM.

entries.title: State-level change rules differ substantially
entries.summary: Some states mandate new comment opportunities whenever substantive changes occur, California often requires 15-day comment for nontrivial changes, Pennsylvania focuses on whether purpose expanded.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some states mandate new comment opportunities whenever substantive changes occur, California often requires 15-day comment for nontrivial changes, Pennsylvania focuses on whether purpose expanded.
entries.legalExplanation: State APA specifics can be stricter or more permissive than federal logical-outgrowth framework.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 252–253
entries.examApplication: Identify actual applicable state's statute; do not automatically use federal § 553 standard.

entries.title: Brocal Corp. v. Pennsylvania DOT, 528 A.2d 114 (Pa. 1987)
entries.summary: Agency could modify transit reimbursement methodology without extending original regulatory purpose and without another comment period.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency could modify transit reimbursement methodology without extending original regulatory purpose and without another comment period.
entries.legalExplanation: Pennsylvania court distinguished same general purpose from changed method even if methodology changed substantially.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 253
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Compare with detailed California new-comment requirement.

topics.title: § 5.3.2 — Disclosure of Supporting Data (pp. 254–259)
topics.description: Nova Scotia, Portland Cement, scientific material in notice-and-comment, competing doctrinal sources, late data, prejudice, OSHA second problem.

entries.title: Scientific foundation must generally be exposed to meaningful criticism
entries.summary: Agencies should disclose central scientific data, key studies and methods supporting a proposed rule so parties can test assumptions and provide informed comments.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies should disclose central scientific data, key studies and methods supporting a proposed rule so parties can test assumptions and provide informed comments.
entries.legalExplanation: You cannot meaningfully challenge a scientific study unless the agency lets you see it.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 254–257
entries.examApplication: Portland Cement doctrine especially in D.C. Circuit often requires critical factual basis to be part of accessible rulemaking record; trade secret and security exceptions can matter.
entries.examTrap: Identify exact unrevealed study, whether central to final rule, whether participants could meaningfully reply, and injury to participation.

entries.title: United States v. Nova Scotia Food Products Corp., 568 F.2d 240 (2d Cir. 1977)
entries.summary: Yes. Core scientific methodology and data needed to be disclosed for informed participation; agency's failure to grapple with economically decisive issue also deficient. Court vacated enforcement injunction and dismissed complaint.
entries.laymanExplanation: Yes. Core scientific methodology and data needed to be disclosed for informed participation; agency's failure to grapple with economically decisive issue also deficient. Court vacated enforcement injunction and dismissed complaint.
entries.legalExplanation: Did FDA's failure to disclose scientific basis and respond to feasibility objections undermine notice-and-comment rulemaking validity, even though manufacturer violated rule's technical terms? Agency expert judgment does not allow material secret factual basis in informal rulemaking. Without access to studies commenters cannot test methodology, evidence relevance, alternative processing standards or harms to whitefish industry; agency must consider important relevant factors.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 254–256
entries.sourceRole: Case opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: FDA prescribed heating/salinity conditions for smoked fish to prevent botulism; Nova Scotia said compliance destroyed marketable hot-smoked whitefish and questioned risks given small historical cases. FDA did not make underlying scientific research and methodology available and neglected commercial feasibility concerns.
entries.issue: Did FDA's failure to disclose scientific basis and respond to feasibility objections undermine notice-and-comment rulemaking validity, even though manufacturer violated rule's technical terms?
entries.holding: Yes. Core scientific methodology and data needed to be disclosed for informed participation; agency's failure to grapple with economically decisive issue also deficient. Court vacated enforcement injunction and dismissed complaint.
entries.reasoning: Agency expert judgment does not allow material secret factual basis in informal rulemaking. Without access to studies commenters cannot test methodology, evidence relevance, alternative processing standards or harms to whitefish industry; agency must consider important relevant factors.
entries.rule: When scientific material underlies proposed rule, disclose critical research to afford meaningful comment and address important concerns in final explanation.
entries.examApplication: Use as example of defense to invalid rule raised during later enforcement; examine both data-disclosure and explanation defects.
entries.examTrap: Do not characterize opinion as demanding that every raw datum be published regardless of relevance or secrets.

entries.title: Portland Cement doctrine and critical factual basis
entries.summary: An agency cannot rest a technical rule on critical factual information known only to itself; material necessary to test proposal should be public and available for refutation.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency cannot rest a technical rule on critical factual information known only to itself; material necessary to test proposal should be public and available for refutation.
entries.legalExplanation: Data and methodology must be disclosed to prevent public comment from becoming guesswork.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 255–257
entries.examApplication: D.C. Circuit foundation Portland Cement; Nova Scotia applies analogous reasoning; later Window Covering rule requires at least most critical material used to support agency position.
entries.examTrap: Assess materiality and whether evidence actually underpinned decision.

entries.title: Portland Cement Association v. Ruckelshaus, 486 F.2d 375 (D.C. Cir. 1973)
entries.summary: Early articulation that technical data and methodology underlying rule should be disclosed for meaningful public testing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Early articulation that technical data and methodology underlying rule should be disclosed for meaningful public testing.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook names scientific-data rule after case.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 255–257
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Distinguish unsupported invention of extra procedures under Vermont Yankee.

entries.title: Window Covering Manufacturers Association v. CPSC, 82 F.4th 1273 (D.C. Cir. 2023)
entries.summary: At least critical material relied upon to defend rule must appear publicly during proceedings and be exposed to refutation.
entries.laymanExplanation: At least critical material relied upon to defend rule must appear publicly during proceedings and be exposed to refutation.
entries.legalExplanation: Modern limiting formulation of the disclosure duty.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 257
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Apply to methodological studies outside docket.

entries.title: The legal basis is contested, particularly after Vermont Yankee
entries.summary: Some opinions ground disclosure in meaningful § 553 comment or arbitrary-capricious review, while Third Circuit in AARP denied that literal § 553 requires all nonpublic underlying information.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some opinions ground disclosure in meaningful § 553 comment or arbitrary-capricious review, while Third Circuit in AARP denied that literal § 553 requires all nonpublic underlying information.
entries.legalExplanation: Policy value of transparent science is clearer than uniform doctrinal rationale.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 257–258
entries.examApplication: Do not present all circuits as identical; note disputes over APA text and tension with judiciary not adding procedures beyond statute.
entries.examTrap: Describe competing interpretation rather than declaring doctrine universally mandatory in every jurisdiction.

entries.title: AARP v. EEOC, 489 F.3d 558 (3d Cir. 2007)
entries.summary: Third Circuit rejected claim § 553 mandated broader public availability of support after agency supplied proposed rule, rationale and comment opportunity.
entries.laymanExplanation: Third Circuit rejected claim § 553 mandated broader public availability of support after agency supplied proposed rule, rationale and comment opportunity.
entries.legalExplanation: Expressly questions Portland Cement's doctrinal breadth.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 257–258
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Flag potential circuit/interpretive disagreement.

entries.title: Rulemaking record and ACUS nonbinding advice
entries.summary: Federal APA does not prescribe exact contents of rulemaking record; ACUS Recommendation 2013–4 provides best practices and agencies commonly post supporting records online.
entries.laymanExplanation: Federal APA does not prescribe exact contents of rulemaking record; ACUS Recommendation 2013–4 provides best practices and agencies commonly post supporting records online.
entries.legalExplanation: Administrative recommendations help organize public records but are not enacted APA obligations by themselves.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 258
entries.examApplication: Differentiate actual statutory/constitutional duties, judicial doctrines and nonbinding ACUS suggestions.

entries.title: Late record additions: responsive support versus new decisive research
entries.summary: Agencies can add supplemental documentation when responding to comments without reopening forever; but materially new outside studies forming decision's basis may trigger a fresh opportunity to comment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies can add supplemental documentation when responding to comments without reopening forever; but materially new outside studies forming decision's basis may trigger a fresh opportunity to comment.
entries.legalExplanation: If late documents only reinforce already debated points, an extra round may be unnecessary; newly decisive analysis should be tested.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 258
entries.examApplication: Rybachek and Kern County allow responsive additions without prejudice; Chamber of Commerce v SEC and American Public Gas emphasize reopening where new external survey or analysis matters.
entries.examTrap: Identify what was known before closure, why it was added, and whether new material changed the premises.

entries.title: Rybachek v. EPA, 904 F.2d 1276 (9th Cir. 1990)
entries.summary: 6,000 pages added after comments did not automatically require endless new comment period.
entries.laymanExplanation: 6,000 pages added after comments did not automatically require endless new comment period.
entries.legalExplanation: Agency responded to prior comments with supporting record materials.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 258
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Distinguish truly new dispositive outside data.

entries.title: Chamber of Commerce v. SEC, 443 F.3d 890 (D.C. Cir. 2006)
entries.summary: SEC relied on new salary/compensation surveys to conclude its mutual-fund governance rule's costs insignificant without re-opening comments; rule set aside.
entries.laymanExplanation: SEC relied on new salary/compensation surveys to conclude its mutual-fund governance rule's costs insignificant without re-opening comments; rule set aside.
entries.legalExplanation: New material on central cost issue needed opportunity for challenge.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 258
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Use to identify prejudice when participants could refute salary figures.

entries.title: Prejudice from nondisclosure
entries.summary: Party generally should identify specific objections or evidence it would offer if material had been disclosed; logical-outgrowth violations may be treated differently.
entries.laymanExplanation: Party generally should identify specific objections or evidence it would offer if material had been disclosed; logical-outgrowth violations may be treated differently.
entries.legalExplanation: To win data nondisclosure challenge, explain what you were prevented from contesting.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 258–259
entries.examApplication: West Virginia v EPA examples demand prejudice; Shell Oil places burden on agency for unanticipated final rule, not necessarily on disappointed commenter.
entries.examTrap: Separate failure to expose scientific data from absent notice of a whole new regulatory question.

entries.title: Shell Oil Co. v. EPA, 950 F.2d 741 (D.C. Cir. 1991)
entries.summary: For logical-outgrowth notice failures, agency must show further public comment on final change would have been useless.
entries.laymanExplanation: For logical-outgrowth notice failures, agency must show further public comment on final change would have been useless.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook contrasts procedural prejudice burden with Portland Cement cases.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 5, pp. 259
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes — opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Do not wrongly impose same burden in each doctrine.
